# Thread Pools on Java Servers

[https://blog.bramp.net/post/2015/12/17/the-importance-of-tuning-your-thread-pools/](https://blog.bramp.net/post/2015/12/17/the-importance-of-tuning-your-thread-pools/)

## Basic Flow of Server

1. Each server has a socket, which waits for TCP connections
2. Accepts TCP connection request
3. Reads data from established connection
4. Parses it, turns it into HTTP request
5. Web app then handles this request

# Types of Servers

## Single Threaded

1. Creates server socket
2. Accepts connections
3. Each request must be fully handled before the next can be accepted

```java
ServerSocket listener = new ServerSocket(8080);
try {
	while (true) {
		Socket socket = listener.accept();
		try {
			handleRequest(socket);
		} catch (IOException e) {
			e.printStackTrace();
		}
	}
} finally {
	listener.close();
}

final static String response =
	"HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\n" +
	"Content-type: text/plain\r\n" +
	"\r\n" +
	"Hello World\r\n";

public static void handleRequest(Socket socket) throws IOException {
	// Read the input stream, and return "200 OK"
	try {
		BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
			new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream()));

		log.info(in.readLine());

		OutputStream out = socket.getOutputStream();
		out.write(response.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
	} finally {
		socket.close();
	}
}
```

## Multi-threaded

### Thread Per Request Approach

```java
public static class HandleRequestRunnable implements Runnable {
	final Socket socket;

	public HandleRequestRunnable(Socket socket) {
		this.socket = socket;
	}

	public void run() {
		try {
			handleRequest(socket);
		} catch (IOException e) {
			e.printStackTrace();
		}
	}
}

// Main loop here
ServerSocket listener = new ServerSocket(8080);
try {
	while (true) {
		Socket socket = listener.accept();
		new Thread( new HandleRequestRunnable(socket) ).start();
	}
} finally {
	listener.close();
}
```

Can cause resource exhaustion, as you're blindly assigning threads to every request.

- Too many requests → too many concurrent threads
- 1000 threads → 1GB JVM RAM for thread Stacks
- Each thread creating objects on Heap
- Heap space exceeds → GC pressure → Thrashing → OOM error
- Other resources that threads use are finite too Eg. File handles, database connections
- Some Calculations for Resource Exhaustion
    
    Each thread requires a certain amount of memory for the stack. On 64bit JVMs, the [default stack size](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/tools/unix/java.html) is 1024KB. If the server receives a flood of requests, or the handleRequest method becomes slow, the server may end up with huge number of concurrent threads. 
    To manage 1000 concurrent requests, the 1000 threads would consume 1GB of the JVM’s RAM just for thread’s stacks. In addition the code executing in each thread will be creating objects on the heap needed to process the request. This very quickly adds up, and can exceed the heap space assigned to the JVM, putting pressure on the garbage collector, causing thrashing and eventually leading to [OutOfMemoryErrors](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/lang/OutOfMemoryError.html).
    

Solution is to use Thread Pools

### Thread Pools

```java
ServerSocket listener = new ServerSocket(8080);
ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
try {
	while (true) {
		Socket socket = listener.accept();
		executor.submit( new HandleRequestRunnable(socket) );
	}
} finally {
	listener.close();
}
```

- Make a thread pool from which threads will be picked to do tasks
- Each task is handled as a Runnable that is submitted to threads

Two kinds of thread pools

1. **NewFixedThreadPool**: bounds the number of threads in the pool
2. **NewCachedThreadPool**: creates unbounded number of threads Usually used on CPU bound – short lived – non IO – not blocked on external resources – kind of requests

[ThreadPoolExecutors](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/java/util/concurrent/ThreadPoolExecutor.html) can be constructed directly, allowing for its behaviour to be customised. For example, the min and max number of threads within the pool can be defined, as well as policies for when threads are created and destroyed. An example of this is shown shortly.

## Work Queue

Work queues in thread pooled servers

- Say all threads are busy - request comes in
- This is added to a thread safe (blocking) queue
- Holding request in queue, cheaper than holding thread (no thread context, no stack/heap memory), even unbounded queues don’t go to resource exhaustion as fast as thread-per-request
- We should bound size of queue

If request comes when queue is full, we can either

1. **DiscardPolicy**: discard the request
2. **AbortPolicy**: throw an exception
3. **CallerRuns**: let the calling (main thread here) fulfill the request, thereby blocking it from further requests. This is not ideal since main thread should never be blocked.

**DISCLAIMER** Queue should only be used to smooth out

- Burst of request
- Stall of processing

And not to try and serve all requests, as that will slow everything down.

```java
public static ExecutorService newBoundedFixedThreadPool(int nThreads, int capacity) {
	return new ThreadPoolExecutor(nThreads, nThreads,
		0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
		new LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>(capacity),
		new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy());
}

public static void boundedThreadPoolServerSocket() throws IOException {
	ServerSocket listener = new ServerSocket(8080);
	ExecutorService executor = newBoundedFixedThreadPool(4, 16);
	try {
		while (true) {
			Socket socket = listener.accept();
			executor.submit( new HandleRequestRunnable(socket) );
		}
	} finally {
		listener.close();
	}
}
```

## How many threads?

Very obious law : **Littles Law** 

![](Thread%20Pools%20on%20Java%20Servers/littlelaw.png)

[](data:image/png;base64,)

L the number of requests in-flight, λ the rate at which new requests arrive, and W the average time to handle the request

- Too few threads -> under utilisation of reqources
- Too many threads -> resource exhaustion – cascading failure

## Dangers of not tuning parameters

- Local resources can be exhausted
- Can also adversely impact others. Suppose many apps query same backend DB. DBs have limit on the number of concurrent connections. If one unbounded app consumes all these connections it will cause an outage.
- A cascading failure could occur. Suppose one instance in a cluster is under load and JVM fills up; load will increase on other instances in the cluster, causing them to fail too.

## How many thread pools?

- In microservices, many backends are called
- One backend can get latent → making threadpool hit it's limit - and requests to get dropped
- **SOLUTION** All requests might not need this backend → create separate thread pools for each backend.
- This backend getting latent now does not affect other thread pools
- Using multiple pools → mitigates deadlocks

## Best Practices

Ensure there is a deadline on all remote calls.

Deadlines on threads; terminate threads processing one request for longer than a defined deadline.

Failing fast; if the backend has failed, the thread pool will quickly fill up with requests waiting for the backend. Instead, flag backend as unhealthy and fail all subsequent requests. Have mechanism to determine when it’s healthy again

If need to call multiple backends, call them parallely instead of sequentially.

Luckily, there is a great library, [hystrix](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix), which packages many of these best practices and exposes them in a simple and safe way.
